title: We spent thousands on a Tui river cruise but ended up on coach trips
description: David Mallon and a group of five others were due to travel on 21 September. But they decided the new itinerary presented to them a few days before dep
body: David Mallon and a group of five others were due to travel on 21 September. But they decided the new itinerary presented to them a few days before departure was so different from what they had booked that they didn't want to go."What they were planning to give us was not a cruise but a glorified coach trip," says David.One reason for not wanting to accept the new plan was that a member of the group was meant to be avoiding long periods of sitting down - such as coach journeys - for health reasons.With no offer of a refund, the group booked a last-minute holiday to Kos instead and decided to try and claim money back on their return."We don't blame Tui for the water levels, but it's the way they've handled the consequences of that," David says.He has now submitted a complaint to Tui and says he will take his quest for a refund to the small claims court if necessary. The BBC contacted Tui River Cruises about passengers' unhappiness with the extensive itinerary changes and the fact they were not offered any refund.  In a statement, a spokesperson said: "Extreme heat across Europe this summer caused low water levels on the Danube, affecting river cruise operators across the region. We review every sailing individually with our nautical partners."Customers on the Tui Isla departures on 14 and 21 September were sent revised itineraries before travelling. Where the ship couldn't sail sections of the river, we arranged coach transfers, hotel stays and adjusted travel arrangements to minimise transfer times so customers could still visit destinations, including Budapest, Vienna and Bratislava."We reviewed the revised arrangements carefully and customers continued their holiday on the amended itinerary under our standard booking conditions. While customers were still able to visit the key destinations on their itinerary, we're sorry some did not get the river cruise experience they had anticipated."

schema.headline: We spent thousands on a Tui river cruise but ended up on coach trips

title: Three people killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports, officials say
description: Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports over two days, authorities said, as flare-up of fighting spilled across the Yemen bo
body: Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports over two days, authorities said, as flare-up of fighting spilled across the Yemen border into the kingdom. Two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (Gaca) said in a statement on Wednesday.In a separate incident, one person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, it added. The attacks, which the Houthis have claimed responsibility for, mark an escalation in the renewed war between the Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.The two airports were attacked on 6 and 7 October, according to Gaca, which did not specify when each airport was hit.Two women, of Moroccan and Algerian nationalities, were killed during the Abha airport attack, near the Yemen border, according to Gaca. Meanwhile, a male resident of Sudanese nationality was killed at King Khalid airport, it added. The country's civil aviation authority did not name who was responsible for the attacks, but Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said its armed forces had attacked both Saudi Arabia airports with ballistic missiles and drones.The Houthi military spokesperson also said the Houthis attacked Aden's International Airport in Yemen on Wednesday. The airport is a main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control and has been repeatedly targeted when fighting erupts in the country. Saree said the two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours". The civil war in Yemen has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west, seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive. That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.But Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.They also declared an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis.In a statement issued late on Wednesday, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports "will not go unpunished".The spokesperson said the Saudi coalition had targeted more than 80 Houthi military sites across "governorates of Saada, Al Hudaydah, Al Jawf and Ma'rib".The Saudi-led coalition formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government. A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres has condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting".Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed on both sides since the latest Houthis' advance.The UN said on Wednesday more than 200,000 people have been displaced by the escalation.

schema.headline: Three people killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports, officials say

title: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK
description: Figure caption, Dame Julia Hoggett says negative sentiment about the UK market has pushed companies to leave in the pastByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsThe UK
body: Figure caption, Dame Julia Hoggett says negative sentiment about the UK market has pushed companies to leave in the pastByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsThe UK needs to do more back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC.Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth.Over the last few years, scores of big firms have left the London market, are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors.The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations.'Take the handbrake off'"If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so," Dame Julia told the BBC's Big Boss podcast."We need to take the handbrake off." The LSE's main market is made up of around 930 companies with a total market value of about £4.9 trillion.Almost 40% are international businesses, hailing from over 80 countries.But in the last few years, many firms have delisted or moved away from the LSE, including takeaway chain Just Eat, which joined the Amsterdam stock exchange,  travel giant Tui which opted for Frankfurt, and Paddy Power-owner Flutter which now trades in New York.'Stop throwing shade'Meanwhile, the number of companies newly listing their shares in London has dwindled.Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.It has coincided in a big rise of UK investment money flowing into US stocks in search of better returns."We talk as a nation about wanting growth in every postcode, but at the moment, a lot of us are funding growth in every zip code," Dame Julia said.There was "no shortage of great companies and no shortage of capital", she added.But negative sentiment about the UK market - which was often exaggerated - had contributed to companies leaving in the past, she said."We need to stop throwing shade at ourselves as a nation... it's a national habit." Big Boss Interview: LSE's Dame Julia HoggettThe boss of the London Stock Exchange speaks to the BBC about the attraction of the UK as a place for companies to list.However, she said British people needed more "incentives" to invest in UK stocks.She wants the government to scrap the 0.5% tax, external Britons pay when they purchase UK shares, pointing out there is no tax when they buy foreign stocks.She also supports the idea of tax credits for Britons investing domestically. The UK had such a scheme until 2016.Business lobbying group the Confederation of British Industry has called for urgent action to halt the exodus of firms from the London Stock Exchange.It said that lighter regulation, better marketing and incentives for investors were needed to stem the outflow.The government declined to say if stock market reform would be part of its Budget this month."As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals," a spokesman said.

schema.headline: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK

title: Conservatives united behind Kemi Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters
description: It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now.Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up
body: It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now.Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up in Birmingham.It is a party very much united around her, with no murmurings of dissent about her leadership, which is quite the contrast from a year ago.The pivot point in her time as Conservative leader so far came in her address to this same gathering 12 months back, when, amid constant chatter about the prospect of Robert Jenrick seeking to topple her, she won over the party faithful with an address that oozed confidence.Not just that. Us reporters were given her speech script, allowing us to follow it line-by-line to help us report what she has said quickly and accurately. But there was a page missing towards the end. On that page was the Conservative crowd pleaser of a plan to scrap stamp duty in England and Northern Ireland.Fast forward to now and there was a familiar drill. There was plenty of chat throughout the conference and beforehand of a new policy coming on inheritance tax, and, sure enough, another page was missing towards the end of her speech with her plan on that.The plan reopens the fascinating politics and psychology of inheritance tax – which is paid by fewer than one in 20 people, external but has been described as the country's most unpopular tax, external. Why so? Advocates of cutting or scrapping it say it is because plenty aspire to one day being rich enough to end up having to pay it, plus it is a second tax on already taxed income.But the Conservatives' opponents, even before this speech, were already looking forward to the argument they anticipated after it. Reform UK, for instance, claim it is a "tax cut for multi-millionaires" and that their plan to cut income tax for millions by raising the threshold at which most people start paying it will benefit far more people.The Institute For Fiscal Studies said the "biggest beneficiaries" would be "a very well off group, external, mainly living in London and the south east of England". It also said it would "encourage wealthy people to buy (or stay in) more expensive homes in their later years". The proportion of estates subject to inheritance tax is rising rapidly, the IFS said, but forecasts are uncertain because it depends on, among other things, what happens to house prices. The Conservatives estimate their inheritance policy change would cost around £6bn a year. They claim to have identified £71bn pounds worth of cuts that can be made to government spending, including £36bn a year from benefits and welfare. The largest savings are projected to come from reforming sickness and disability benefits, where the party believes it can save £13.7bn a year, with £9.5bn a year from ending access to benefits for non-EU nationals, £4.5bn from changes to housing benefit, and £3.1bn from reintroducing the two-child limit for Universal Credit.But Work and Pensions Minister Torsten Bell said "history is very clear that promising this scale of tax cuts ends one way, external: trashing your public finances".Policy announcements aside, what stood out in this speech for me was a broader point. The veteran Conservative elections strategist Sir Lynton Crosby once suggested the party ought to "scrape the barnacles off the boat" as he put it, in reference to unpopular policies that could cause the Tories a headache during an election campaign.This speech felt like Badenoch revelling in pointing at the clean hull of the Conservative ship, what she sees as those barnacles removed, not least the high-profile defections of Jenrick and Suella Braverman.There was a striking glee and anger in her reflections about Reform UK. She sought to portray them as sleazy and pointedly decided to lean into an argument of recent months about Englishness.Braverman has argued that, given her Asian heritage, "I'm not English". "I'm proud to be British. My family and ancestors have a link to Britain which spans centuries. But in no way are we English," she wrote on social media last month, external, adding: "Englishness is an ethnicity."Badenoch expressed her personal fury at this, saying that as the mother of mixed-race children "I don't want to explain to my son, when we're watching our brilliant England team play football, that some people don't think our black players are English".The recurring message, today and over the last few days, is Badenoch cannot stand Reform and won't work with them before or after the next general election.But what she said amounted to an attack on Reform's character and the judgement of their prominent figures, rather than a significant focus on the policies we hear talked about most often by Nigel Farage.Badenoch did talk about immigration, but not at length. She largely left the issue – and the Conservative policy to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights, as Reform also advocates - to her shadow home secretary Chris Philp who spoke before her.Instead, Badenoch grounded this speech in the big picture tussle to be trusted between Labour and the Conservatives – and in particular who was better placed to deliver a growing economy.In tone, language and public enthusiasm for the argument, Badenoch and Andy Burnham are quite the contrast with their immediate predecessors Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer. Badenoch and Burnham both look like they are enjoying themselves on the stage, and are both enthusiastic purveyors of the core of what are their very different worldviews.Badenoch acknowledged this with what she called the "battle for the soul of this nation" in the opening minute or so of her address. It is a trailer for the debate to come this autumn and beyond.The Conservatives feel chipper and are united. But while both of these things are better than the alternative for any party leader, they are not the same as being popular.And, as Kemi Badenoch acknowledged, they are not there on that score yet, by a long chalk, with opinion polls suggesting they are more unpopular than when they were annihilated at the last general election.The numbers, for them, are dire. Just not as bad, relatively speaking, as they were.But they hope things are looking up for them: Reform has had a bruising few months, and Labour, they believe, are leaning to the Left, trying to lure Green and Liberal Democrat supporters towards them.Can the Conservatives also lure recent Lib Dem supporters in the south of England with talk of help with childcare costs whatever your income, not hiking the council tax of very expensive homes and this inheritance tax plan?This, Tories hope, there are now gaps in the political market they can exploit.They crave catching and overtaking Reform in the polls, in the hope that after that there is a tipping point allowing them to credibly claim they are the most viable alternative to a Labour or Labour-led future government. Let's see.

schema.headline: Conservatives united behind Kemi Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters

title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
description: An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, a
body: An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases. The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital."We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".Union spokesperson Alicia del Río said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".A cause of death was not announced.Abascal's death was received in Puerta del Sol with a big collective gasp, then followed by a minute of silence.It is in this square in the centre of Madrid where thousands have been camping since Abascal's eviction last month to demand more affordable housing.On Wednesday, it became the place to pay tribute to her.People lit dozens of candles around the square in a small improvised vigil that glowed with a warm light on a dry and warm autumn night.Other candles formed an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government.Messages on cardboard banners next to the candles read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Mari Carmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others.A few hundred people then took to the streets that connect Puerta del Sol with the Spanish Congress, just 500m away, in an improvised protest.During the march people chanted: "We will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Mari Carmen is still alive". There were other chants against fascism and against the police.The police had set up barriers to block the march. There was not a big police presence, and there was the tension that protests sometimes have.Many protesters seemed to feel the police have been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices.After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers".Wednesday night's march has finished, but the camping, already on its 12th night, will continue "as long as necessary" one of the protesters told the BBC.Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.However, Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high"."Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours'," it said.In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs.""All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also sent his condolences to Maricarmen's loved ones, as he said on X: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall."In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added.Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.On Monday Sánchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.Speaking on Monday, Sánchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.

schema.headline: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says

title: New York court hears arguments in ongoing 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia
description: Bayoumi, who is now retired from government work, has denied knowing the two men were hijackers or that he had any involvement in 9/11, while Saudi Ar
body: Bayoumi, who is now retired from government work, has denied knowing the two men were hijackers or that he had any involvement in 9/11, while Saudi Arabia has said that any allegation that it or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.The Kingdom has argued that, as a foreign sovereign state, it has immunity from prosecution in US courts.The families, who first filed the lawsuit in 2002, spent several years lobbying US Congress to pass an amendment to the foreign sovereign immunity law to allow the case to go ahead. In 2016, Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), which allows civil claims against a foreign state or official for injuries, death, or damages from an act of international terrorism.In August 2025, the Manhattan District Court ruled that the 9/11 families had presented enough evidence to meet the terms of the act and the case was allowed to proceed towards a trial. Saudi Arabia on Wednesday asked the Court of Appeals to reverse that decision. Counsel Gregory Rapawy argued core issues of fact – including the central question of the nature of Bayoumi's employment by the Saudi state – had not been decided and needed to be done so before the country could be stripped of immunity.9/11 families' lawyer Gavin Simpson argued that the District Court had already found that Bayoumi's actions "were not just acts of a good Samaritan or an innocent participant". "He was, in fact, following Saudi Arabia's instructions when assisting the hijackers," said Simpson, and that these were points that Saudi Arabia had "failed to rebut."One option the judges seemed to wrestle with was whether to send the case back to the district court to make more concrete findings, which could involve taking testimony from live witnesses.Asked by Judge Guido Calabresi which witnesses Saudi Arabia could call in that eventuality, Rapawy suggested that if the issue ultimately came down to Bayoumi's credibility, "we would have to see" if he could be called to testify.As he drew the hearing to a close, Judge William Nardini said "it's a difficult case, and we will take it under advisement", meaning that the panel would issue a ruling at a future date.Speaking outside the courthouse, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom was killed in the World Trade Center, told the BBC she felt positive about the hearing. "25 years is an extraordinary time to go without accountability and justice for the murder of your loved one. What we hope is that the judges will uphold [District Court] Judge Daniels' decision and move to a trial."

schema.headline: New York court hears arguments in ongoing 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia

title: Declan Rice contract: Arsenal and England midfielder close to agreeing new deal
description: Declan Rice is close to agreeing a new long-term Arsenal contract, sources have told BBC Sport.The England midfielder has become a crucial player for
body: Declan Rice is close to agreeing a new long-term Arsenal contract, sources have told BBC Sport.The England midfielder has become a crucial player for the Gunners since his arrival from West Ham for £105m in July 2023.His current deal expires at the end of next season but BBC Sport revealed in March that talks over a new contract were under way with the process now at an advanced stage.The 27-year-old has made 165 appearances for Arsenal and helped the club end their 22-year wait for a Premier League title last term. Rice would receive a significant increase to his reported £240,000-per-week salary, putting him on a par with the club's best earner Bukayo Saka, who is believed to be paid about £350,000 a week.While Rice withdrew from Thomas Tuchel's England squad before the recent three-week camp, he has amassed 80 caps since switching his international allegiance from the Republic of Ireland in 2019.Tuchel has also previously lauded him one of the "best midfielders in Europe".Rice is expected to be involved for Arsenal when they host Leeds in the English top flight on Saturday (12:30 BST).The news comes after Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta's new four-year deal with the Premier League champions was announced on Wednesday.

schema.headline: Declan Rice contract: Arsenal and England midfielder close to agreeing new deal

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Kemi's family home pledge' and 'Badenoch invokes core Tory values'
description: Most of the front pages lead with Kemi Badenoch's Conservative conference speech yesterday. "We're ready for the fight", external" is the Daily Telegr
body: Most of the front pages lead with Kemi Badenoch's Conservative conference speech yesterday. "We're ready for the fight", external" is the Daily Telegraph's verdict on the Tory leader's message. The Financial Times, external says her promises to cut taxes represent a return to core Conservative values, but the Guardian describes them as "prioritising the wealthiest", external. The Daily Express believes Badenoch is a "no nonsense" leader, external - a phrase used by several papers - and that she heads a party that will stop what it describes as inheritance tax "raids". The Times says the Conservatives are now focused on wooing "Middle England"., external"Reform not dodgy, says Reform", external is the Daily Mirror's review of the party's internal investigation finding it did not breach electoral law, when senior officials were recorded by an undercover journalist discussing foreign donations. The paper describes the probe as a "white wash".The i reports that a major government review will call for schoolchildren to be given help for ADHD,, external autism and mental health issues even before they are diagnosed. The paper says the report will also question whether the conditions are being over-diagnosed and recommend community-based support.The Guardian warns that the government's reforms to the special education system , externalin England could "unravel" because parents are rushing to secure support before any changes are implemented. It says experts are now urging ministers to review the timeline for their plans, which they claim are based on optimistic assumptions. The Department for Education says it's committed to implementing its plans by 2030.A new daily pill could represent the biggest Parkinson's breakthrough, external since the 1960s, according to the Times. It says a clinical trial of Solengepras found it reduced patients' stiffness, slowness and tremors, as well as keeping them more alert.The Telegraph says scientists could have found a key to helping us live longer in a 194-year-old giant tortoise , externalcalled Jonathan. He lives on the island of St Helena in the South Atlantic and is estimated to have hatched in 1832. Researchers say he has the "super genes" of a 5-year-old that reduce inflammation, regulate insulin and suppress cancer.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Kemi's family home pledge' and 'Badenoch invokes core Tory values'

title: Fifa: Ex-Spurs player Ramon Vega intends to stand in 2027 presidential election
description: Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election.The 55-year-old is the
body: Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election.The 55-year-old is the first person to confirm they want to challenge Gianni Infantino, who has defied calls to step down in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, which has sparked a major backlash across football.A former Switzerland centre-back, Vega also played for Celtic and Watford and has worked in finance since retiring from football in 2004."I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise Fifa for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs," he said.Meanwhile, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa - president of the Asian Football Confederation - has written to Infantino, distancing himself from an external review of Fifa's governance system.In his letter - seen by BBC Sport - Sheikh Salman proposes that Fifa's council sets up a working group to examine potential reforms, "rather than being outsourced to an external party".Last month, Infantino said he was "fully committed to leading Fifa" despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to quit.Vega considered running for Fifa's top job in 2015 following the suspension of former president Sepp Blatter.Four years later he said he would stand against Infantino, but failed to garner enough support to be included in the ballot, having required the backing of five of Fifa's 211 member federations. Candidates must also be proposed by a member association and have played an active role in the game for two of the past five years, as well as passing an eligibility check by a review committee. "I am standing because my life has prepared me to serve the game," Vega said in a statement announcing his candidacy."Football does not belong to presidents, confederations or administrators. Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution."It is the people's game and belongs to everyone: the players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life."It belongs to every child discovering the game, every professional carrying the hopes of a nation, and the billions of supporters whose passion makes football the world's game."Football must always come first. Yet for too long, division has fractured our football family."The current leadership has demoralised the game. Weak governance has damaged Fifa's credibility and eroded trust across the global football family. We must stop this conflict from escalating."Ego-driven battles within football administration must never be allowed to damage those who matter most: the players, coaches, referees and supporters around the world. They are not responsible for these conflicts. They deserve better."Vega concluded: "Football is in the emergency room, on life support. We cannot wait any longer. Fifa needs a new direction and fundamental reform."We must reunite the football family, restore trust, bring stability and modernise Fifa's governance. This requires decisive change - not cosmetic adjustments."It comes with Sheikh Salman appearing to soften his stance towards Infantino just two months after the AFC president signed a joint letter with the heads of Uefa and Concacaf accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception" over his Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.At the time, the three confederations said any review of Fifa's governance must be "conducted by a fully independent third party".Now, however, Salman says he believes the process should be "driven by the football institutions themselves, rather than being outsourced to an external party".He added: "I believe there is value in taking this opportunity to consider constructively whether Fifa's existing governance arrangements can be strengthened."The issue is not necessarily whether this requires a wholesale redesign of Fifa's governance system."Fifa's council meets in Zurich next week for the first time since the FFE plan emerged in July.

schema.headline: Fifa: Ex-Spurs player Ramon Vega intends to stand in 2027 presidential election

title: 'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells Britain
description: French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to "come all the way" back to the EU, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalled a second
body: French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to "come all the way" back to the EU, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalled a second Brexit referendum was "possible" in a future Labour election manifesto.Lescure said being in the bloc comes with some difficulties, but it enables members to better address the challenges facing the world.Last week, Burnham said the UK needed to "consider the options", ranging from staying as is, rejoining the customs union or single market, or going "all the way".Asked about the PM's comments, Lescure told the BBC: "British people decided, and that's obviously their 100% right, and if they're willing to come back, they will have to decide.""But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime."Burnham recently warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK.The prime minister expressed concerns about how British industry and supply chains could be affected by the planned Made In Europe scheme.The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies. The EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its own supply chains.Asked about the possibility of Britain being kept out of the scheme, Lescure said: "Come back, and you'll be at the table, and we discuss all these things together."

schema.headline: 'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells Britain

title: Pep Guardiola: Former Man City manager to attend PSG Champions League tie
description: Pep Guardiola is expected to attend Manchester City's Champions League tie against Paris St-Germain next week - the club's first home match since they
body: Pep Guardiola is expected to attend Manchester City's Champions League tie against Paris St-Germain next week - the club's first home match since they were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.It will mark the first time the Spaniard has returned to Etihad Stadium since he left the club at the end of last season after a decade as manager.Earlier this month, an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.City continue to deny any wrongdoing and have lodged an appeal against the findings in the Premier League's report that stated the club falsely inflated commercial revenues by £830m through "sham" contracts.In the aftermath of the verdict, 55-year-old Guardiola backed City's owners and leadership and says he will "always" be behind the club."I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here; more than ever," he posted on social media."I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano], the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters."Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."

schema.headline: Pep Guardiola: Former Man City manager to attend PSG Champions League tie

title: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' after failed execution, lawyers say
description: A lawyer for convicted murderer Christa Pike says that she woke up in hospital "angry and confused" after she survived a botched execution attempt las
body: A lawyer for convicted murderer Christa Pike says that she woke up in hospital "angry and confused" after she survived a botched execution attempt last week.Her first words were to ask "Where am I?" and "Who are you?", her lawyer Randy Spivey recalled during a news conference. Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September in Tennessee.Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented, and that no other US inmate has survived a lethal injection from executioners.A court on Wednesday ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care and is being restrained at her hands and feet in her hospital bed, her lawyers said at the news conference after a court hearing on Wednesday. Spivey said that her legal team believed for days that she was brain dead, and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment. However, in a "shock to everyone", she began to talk on Tuesday, while recalling only limited details about the execution attempt.Pike, he said, had helped the execution team find a vein in her arm, and she was kind and polite while she was being injected.Then she woke up in a hospital with a tube down her throat and people she didn't know. Both of her arms, he said, are now "tremendously swollen"."We don't know the toll all of this will take" on her mental health, Spivey said, noting how she was left "angry and confused" by the ordeal.He added that she also has a blood clot in one of her arms, pneumonia, and is not able to swallow.Pike is believed to be the only person to survive an execution attempt by lethal injection. After it became clear Pike would not die, following two rounds of the drug pentobarbital, she was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical.Earlier on Wednesday, lawyers appeared before a judge for an emergency hearing, where her team requested that all evidence from the botched execution be preserved. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.Luke Ihnen, one of Pike's lawyers, began by describing the "roadblocks" that have made it challenging to communicate with his client.  "Up until yesterday our client was unconscious, and unable to communicate," he told Judge Chancellor I'Ashea Myles. Pike is now "speaking limitedly", he said.Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers called attention to the "unusual procedural position here", prompting agreement from the judge. He argued that an emergency motion was unnecessary because the state is already compelled to preserve evidence. Still, Judge Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels.The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt.She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.Asked by the judge whether the state intended to reschedule execution for Pike, Ayers said he did not know the answer. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief said he is resigning after the failed execution.Ihnen asked the judge to allow Pike access to a phone so she can call her lawyers, and they can have "continuous liberal access to Ms Pike". He said they were kept waiting for over two hours during a recent attempt to visit her in hospital.

title: Bank of England reveals the four animals to feature on banknotes
description: Hedgehog among four animals chosen to feature on new banknotesImage source, Bank of England/PA WireByCost of living correspondentBanknotes are getting
body: Hedgehog among four animals chosen to feature on new banknotesImage source, Bank of England/PA WireByCost of living correspondentBanknotes are getting a nature makeover - and the Bank of England has revealed the four creatures that will feature on our money.The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will appear on the redesigned notes in years to come - although no decision has been made about which animal will be shown on which banknote.The owl, bumblebee and hedgehog topped a public vote in their specific categories, and the puffin was included to celebrate marine life, the coastline and bring variety to the notes, the Bank said.Wildlife is replacing notable figures from history, such as Sir Winston Churchill, on our cash in a decision that angered a number of leading politicians.  'Four distinct and inspiring animals'"We have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes," said Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier.A panel of wildlife experts drew up a shortlist of 18 mammals, birds, amphibians insects and fish which were put forward to public nominations. Respondents were invited to select up to six.More than 2.5 million votes were cast by 478,531 people, ranging from wildlife enthusiasts to primary school classes. The buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) was a clear winner, receiving 360,399 votes, nearly 90,000 more than the barn owl (Tyto alba).The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) was most popular in the mammals category.The red fox, in the mammals category, and the common kingfisher, among the birds, received more nominations than the Atlantic puffin. The puffin (Fratercula arctica) was still selected because it was the most popular marine animal. The Bank said its inclusion added variety to the series, made the denominations easier to distinguish, and gave an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline.The puffin and bees also feature on coins, as part of the Royal Mint's redesigned 20p and £1 coins respectively. Image source, Bank of England/PA WireImage caption, Mock-ups of the new Bank of England banknotes featuring all four winners  Each of the quartet of creatures will feature as the central image of a £5, £10, £20 or £50 note, which will also feature other elements from nature as part of their designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The monarch will still feature on the other side of the notes.Rhys Phillips, the Bank's incoming chief cashier who will be responsible for the roll-out of the new series of notes, said the process of designing, testing and printing banknotes could take years.He said the Bank needed to make sure they were high-quality, resilient and accessible. As the designs were only in the very early stages, they would be unveiled closer to their launch."We'll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we've announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science," he said.Wildlife already appears on banknotes in the UK, with mackerel, otters, red squirrels and osprey featuring on notes issued by the Royal Bank of Scotland, external.Figure caption, Churchill's granddaughter happy with his picture being replaced on the £5 noteYet it will be the first time since 1970 that the reverse side of Bank of England notes will no longer feature notable figures from history.On notes circulating currently, in ascending order of value, are former Prime Minister Sir Winston Churchill, author Jane Austen, artist JMW Turner and mathematician and wartime codebreaker Alan Turing.The proposed removal of wartime leader Churchill angered Reform leader Nigel Farage, and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch describing the move as "a silly thing to do".The Bank said the move was primarily to stop counterfeiting so all images needed to be replaced on banknotes over time.

schema.headline: Bank of England reveals the four animals to feature on banknotes

title: What happens next to Christa Pike?
description: What could happen next in Christa Pike's case?Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Christa Pike’s "unprecedented" recovery after failed execution
body: What could happen next in Christa Pike's case?Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Christa Pike’s "unprecedented" recovery after failed executionByBrandon DrenonThe botched execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has thrust Tennessee's criminal justice system into uncharted territory. After state officials administered two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, Pike survived and was transported to a nearby hospital, where she was intubated. Six days later, her lawyers announced she was "conscious and speaking". Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation into what went wrong at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville and suspended all executions for the rest of the year.The fate of Pike, who has been on death row for 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer, now lies in a mysterious grey area.Doctor Joel Zivot, an anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defence team, says he suspects the deadly chemical spread under her skin instead of her bloodstream, and, because of the the large dose, it could take days or even weeks for a clear picture of her health to emerge.At a hearing on Wednesday, an attorney for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.Pike's lawyers are seeking to have Pike's death sentence commuted to a lesser punishment of life in prison without parole.  Lee, who has the power to pardon Pike or commute her sentence, has not indicated what the state will do in her case.The BBC spoke to multiple experts to explore what could happen next.Attempt to execute Pike by lethal injection againThe Tennessee Department of Correction could attempt to execute Pike again by lethal injection, but the state would very likely run into legal challenges based on constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment."For the state to attempt to execute her again using the same methodology, they would have severe legal hurdles," Tennessee-based defence attorney Stephen Ross Johnson said. Johnson said Tennessee had botched two executions in one year  - it also failed to kill Tony Carruthers in May - which could give lawyers the grounds to argue broadly against the constitutionality of the state’s lethal injection protocol. Pike's lawyers could also argue a lethal injection is what Johnson called "unconstitutional as applied", meaning it is cruel and unusual specifically for Pike, due to her medical condition.Pike's lawyers had warned before the execution attempt that she has small veins and thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition that would complicate the procedure. Her medical condition combined with the state's botched execution would make it difficult for Tennessee to present a convincing legal argument for attempting lethal injection again, Johnson said. Attempt to execute her with a different methodBut Johnson, president-elect of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, could see the state attempting an execution by a different method.This would require "additional legal hoops", including approval from the governor's office and potentially the state legislature. Since Pike's survival, political leaders in Tennessee have called for moving her death sentence forward through other means.Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair." Congressman Tim Burchett, posted on social media that he's already filed a bill to "bring back hanging".Tennessee could be allowed to use the electric chair because Pike committed the murder in 1995 before the state changed its execution laws. She would need to waive her right to lethal injection in writing, which means it would have to be her decision, Vanderbilt University law professor Chris Slobogin said.Given Pike's exact medical state is unknown, Slobogin said there is a scenario where the state could be blocked from attempting to execute her again, regardless of method.It is also considered cruel and unusual punishment to execute someone who is mentally incapable of understanding why it is happening, he explained.Historically this has applied to prisoners with dementia or psychosis, but experts have said there is a chance that Pike has suffered brain damage.Commute her sentence Tennessee is taking a long pause on carrying out capital punishment.Only one person was due to be executed this year after Pike, which the governor has now postponed. Earlier, in May, the Carruthers execution was suspended by a year after state officials could not find a vein to administer the lethal injection.That means it will likely take a while for any movement in Pike's case."At a minimum there's going to be some significant delay while this issue is studied by the state", defence attorney Johnson said, adding Pike's health would also need to be studied.Slobogin suspects the governor will commute her sentence, especially if missteps by state officials are uncovered in the investigation he has ordered."If the investigation, in any way, shape, or form, suggests that the protocol was not followed, or is hard to carry out, that might be the easy way for him to go, given the complications with the execution and all the bad press," he said. There is legal precedent for a death sentence to be commuted due to a botched execution combined with an inmate's poor medical state.The execution of Alabama death-row prisoner Doyle Hamm was called off after more than two hours of attempts to establish an IV line failed. The state gave up on executing him following a legal settlement that related, in part, to his health. He later died of natural causes.
